body.x: Most biodatas for daughters are written about them, not with them. A mother, an aunt or a family friend assembles the facts — date of birth, height, degree, father's occupation — and the young woman herself appears in the document as a list of measurements and certificates. Then everyone wonders why the replies feel like inspections. This guide is written from her chair. A biodata that works is one she has helped to write, recognises herself in, and can stand behind in the meetings that follow — because those meetings will be with her, not with the paper.
How your biodata is actually read

Understand the two readings your biodata will get. The first takes under a minute and is usually done by the groom's mother, sister or the matchmaker herself: age, city, sect and practice signals, education, family standing. It is a filter, and it is mostly checking that nothing rules you out. The second reading is slower — often the groom himself, or the family together in the evening — and it is looking for a person: Is she serious? Is she settled? Would conversation with her be easy? Would she fit the rhythm of this household, and would we fit hers?

Write for both readings. The filter facts must be complete, accurate and easy to find — a missing age or an unclear city gets a biodata set aside, not chased. But the second reading is where matches are actually made, and it rewards the things a certificate list cannot carry: how she spends her time, what she is building towards, what her practice looks like in ordinary weeks. Two or three concrete lines do more than a paragraph of adjectives.
Lead with education, practice and character

Open with the woman, in this order: who she is and where she is based; her education and what she is doing with it now — a job, a training year, a business, further study, or a deliberate pause, stated without embarrassment; then her practice, described concretely rather than in slogans. "Prays five times, wears hijab, attends the majlis in Muharram and teaches at the Saturday school" tells a family more than "religious and homely" ever will. Add languages, the community she belongs to, and one or two true details of character — she runs the family's accounts, she has cared for a grandparent, she organises the local charity collection. Specifics are believable; superlatives are not.

And the fields everyone asks about that shrink a person to a body — height, weight, complexion? You cannot stop some readers filtering on them, and pretending otherwise helps no one. But you can refuse to headline them. Give the plain facts in one unadorned line, in their proper place, with no salesmanship: no "fair and slim", no apology, no embellishment. A family whose first enthusiasm is a complexion has told you something important about itself — and a biodata written with dignity quietly filters those families out before they can waste her time.
The photograph: decide the rules before anyone asks

Photographs travel further and live longer than biodatas, so settle the order of things in advance. A workable order, used by many careful families: the biodata goes first; photographs follow only after the other family has read it, shown genuine interest, and named who they are. The photo passes from her mother or wali to their counterpart — one named person, not a group admin, not a chain of cousins. On Shia Rishta the same principle is built in: profile photographs stay private until the account holder chooses to share them, and a family can mirror that discipline offline.

Practical habits that protect her: send recent, ordinary photographs — daylight, no studio glamour, no heavy filters — because the person in the meeting must match the person in the picture. State the expectation at the moment of sending: this is for your family's viewing, please do not forward it, and please delete it if things do not proceed. Some families watermark images or send them in a view-once format; the method matters less than the principle, which is consent at every step. Asking for deletion after a no is not rudeness. It is the agreement, and families who resist it have answered a question about themselves.
Say what she is looking for — plainly, and without apology

The expectations section is where daughters are most often edited into vagueness, usually by loving parents who fear she will sound demanding. Resist it. A clear statement of what she is looking for — a practising husband, a city she can realistically move to, her intention to continue working or studying after marriage, the living arrangement she hopes for — is not arrogance. It is the information the other family needs to say an honest yes or no, and every month saved from a mismatch is a month of her life returned.

Plain does not mean rigid. Separate the essentials from the preferences: "must be practising and settled in the UK" is a condition; "a family in the Midlands would be easier" is a preference. Marking which is which makes her look serious rather than fussy — and serious is exactly the impression that draws serious families.
Her no is part of the document

Finally, the part no template includes: she approves the final version before it circulates anywhere, and she can stop any conversation, at any stage, without supplying a reason that satisfies the whole family. A biodata is an introduction, not a commitment. Parents — your role in this document is amplifier and shield: you lend her your network, your verification and your protection, but the voice should be hers. If she reads the finished page and does not recognise herself, rewrite it until she does.

That is the whole secret of a biodata that works. It does not perform a daughter; it presents a person — educated, practising, clear about what she wants, careful with her own image, and free to decline. Families worth joining can tell the difference within one reading, and those are the only replies worth having.
